course.title: Medical Terminology
course.description: Medical terminology is the specialized language that health professionals use to name the parts of the body, their conditions, and the procedures done to them with precision. This foundations course shows how nearly every term is built from a small set of word parts - roots, prefixes, suffixes, and combining vowels - so an unfamiliar word can be decoded instead of memorized one at a time. Structure and topics are adapted from the Medical terminology overview on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The part of a medical term that carries its core meaning, usually a body part, is called the...
questions.explanation: The word root holds the central meaning, such as 'cardi' for heart - see 'How medical terms are built'.

questions.prompt: In the term 'cardiology,' the letter 'o' between 'cardi' and 'logy' is a...
questions.explanation: A combining vowel, almost always 'o', links a root to a suffix or to another root.

questions.prompt: The prefix 'tachy-' means...
questions.explanation: 'Tachy-' means fast, so tachycardia is a rapid heart rate.

questions.prompt: The suffix '-itis' means...
questions.explanation: '-itis' means inflammation, so hepatitis is inflammation of the liver.

questions.prompt: The combining form 'nephr/o' refers to the...
questions.explanation: 'Nephr/o' means kidney; a nephrectomy is removal of a kidney.

questions.prompt: The term 'hepatectomy' means surgical removal of the...
questions.explanation: 'Hepat' is liver and '-ectomy' is surgical removal, so it is removal of the liver.

questions.prompt: A patient with 'bradycardia' has a heart rate that is...
questions.explanation: 'Brady-' means slow, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate.

questions.prompt: The sagittal plane divides the body into...
questions.explanation: The sagittal plane makes a left-right division; a midsagittal cut gives equal halves.

lessons.title: How medical terms are built: word parts and combining vowels
lessons.grammar_note: Keep the combining vowel (usually 'o') between two roots, and before a suffix that starts with a consonant; drop it before a suffix that starts with a vowel - so cardi/o + logy becomes cardiology, but cardi + itis becomes carditis.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the four building blocks of a medical term, explain what a combining form is, and read a term by breaking it into its pieces. By the end you will be able to take a word you have never met, such as pericarditis, and reason out its meaning rather than guess at it. The payoff is large: a few dozen word parts combine into thousands of terms, so learning the parts replaces memorizing endless whole words. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in the word cardiology, which piece carries the core meaning of heart, and which piece tells you it names a field of study? Hold those two answers in mind, because the rest of this lesson gives you a reliable method for pulling any term apart into exactly these kinds of pieces and then reading them back in the right order.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most medical terms are built from up to four parts. The word root carries the core meaning and is usually a body part, such as cardi (heart), hepat (liver), or neur (nerve). A prefix is attached to the front and often signals location, number, time, or negation, such as peri- (around) or hypo- (below normal). A suffix is attached to the end and often names a condition, a procedure, or a specialty, such as -itis (inflammation) or -ectomy (surgical removal). A combining vowel, nearly always the letter o, is a connector with no meaning of its own; it makes the word easier to say. A root joined to its combining vowel is written as a combining form, such as cardi/o. The guiding rule is simple: keep the combining vowel between two roots, and keep it before a suffix that begins with a consonant, but drop it before a suffix that begins with a vowel. That single rule explains why we say cardiology but carditis.

sections.heading: Key parts & examples
sections.text: To decode a term, work from the end toward the front, then fill in the middle. Start with the suffix, because it usually tells you what kind of thing the word names - a condition, a procedure, or a study. Next read the prefix, which modifies the meaning. Finally read the root or roots in the center. Take pericarditis: the suffix -itis means inflammation, the prefix peri- means around, and the root cardi means heart, so the whole word means inflammation of the tissue around the heart. Take gastroenterology: two roots, gastr (stomach) and enter (intestine), are joined by the combining vowel o, and the suffix -logy means study of, giving the study of the stomach and intestines. Notice the vowel is kept between the two roots and kept before -logy, which starts with a consonant. Now compare neuritis: the root neur meets the suffix -itis, which starts with a vowel, so the combining vowel is dropped, giving inflammation of a nerve.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four possible parts of a medical term. 2) In cardiology, which part is the suffix and what does it mean? 3) Build a word for inflammation of the liver from hepat and -itis - do you keep or drop the combining vowel? 4) Decode osteoarthritis into its parts. 5) Why does gastroenterology keep the o but neuritis does not? Answers: 1) word root, prefix, suffix, and combining vowel. 2) -logy (also written -ology), meaning study of. 3) Drop it, because -itis starts with a vowel, giving hepatitis. 4) oste (bone) + arthr (joint) + -itis (inflammation), inflammation of bone and joint. 5) The o is kept between the two roots in gastroenterology, but dropped before the vowel-starting suffix -itis in neuritis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to memorize whole terms as if each were unrelated, when nearly all share a small kit of parts you can reuse. Mistake: keeping the combining vowel before a suffix that starts with a vowel, which produces wrong forms like gastroitis instead of gastritis. Mistake: reading a term front to back; the suffix at the end is usually the fastest clue to what the word names. Exit: (a) When do you drop the combining vowel? (b) In which order should you read the parts of an unfamiliar term? Answers: drop it before a suffix that begins with a vowel, but keep it between two roots and before a consonant-starting suffix; read the suffix first, then the prefix, then the root or roots in the middle.

lessons.title: Common word roots and combining forms
lessons.grammar_note: Some structures have both a Greek and a Latin root - the kidney is nephr/o (Greek) and ren/o (Latin) - and the choice often depends on the ending, as in nephrology but renal.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize a core set of word roots for major body parts and turn each root into a combining form. These roots appear again and again, so learning them now pays off in every later lesson. By the end you will be able to look at a combining form such as cardi/o, hepat/o, or neur/o and say at once what structure it names, and then combine it with a suffix to make a real term. Warm-up: the word dermatology names the medical specialty for which organ? Hold that answer, because skin is one of the roots on today's list, and by the close of the lesson you should be able to build and break several terms that use it, along with roots for the heart, liver, kidney, bone, nerve, stomach, joint, muscle, and blood.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A manageable set of roots covers most everyday clinical language. For the heart, cardi/o; for the liver, hepat/o; for the kidney, nephr/o (and the Latin ren/o); for bone, oste/o; for skin, derm/o and dermat/o; for a nerve, neur/o. Add a few more that appear constantly: gastr/o for the stomach, enter/o for the intestine, arthr/o for a joint, my/o for muscle, and hem/o or hemat/o for blood. Each root becomes a combining form when you attach its combining vowel, almost always o, written with a slash as cardi/o. The combining form is the version you actually use when you join the root to a suffix that starts with a consonant or to another root. When the suffix starts with a vowel, you set the combining vowel aside and use the plain root. Learning roots as combining forms makes both building and decoding terms faster, because the connector is already attached and ready.

sections.heading: Key parts & examples
sections.text: Watch the roots turn into real words. Cardi/o plus -logy gives cardiology, the study of the heart. Hepat plus -itis gives hepatitis, inflammation of the liver, with the vowel dropped before the vowel-starting suffix. Nephr plus -ectomy gives nephrectomy, surgical removal of a kidney, while ren/o plus -al gives renal, meaning relating to the kidney. Oste/o plus -porosis gives osteoporosis, a condition of porous, weakened bone. Dermat/o plus -logy gives dermatology, the study of the skin. Neur plus -itis gives neuritis, inflammation of a nerve, and neur/o plus -logy gives neurology. Gastr plus -itis gives gastritis, inflammation of the stomach lining. Arthr plus -itis gives arthritis, inflammation of a joint. My/o plus -algia (pain) gives myalgia, muscle pain. Hemat/o plus -logy gives hematology, the study of blood. Each example simply snaps a known root onto a known suffix and applies the combining-vowel rule.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Give the combining form for the heart and the kidney. 2) What does neur/o mean? 3) Build a word for the study of the skin. 4) Decode gastritis into its parts. 5) Which two roots name the kidney, and when is each used? 6) What does hematology study? Answers: 1) cardi/o for the heart and nephr/o for the kidney. 2) a nerve. 3) dermat/o + -logy, dermatology. 4) gastr (stomach) + -itis (inflammation), inflammation of the stomach. 5) nephr/o (Greek, as in nephrology) and ren/o (Latin, as in renal); the choice usually follows the ending. 6) blood, from hemat/o (blood) and -logy (study of).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing similar-looking roots, such as neur/o (nerve) with nephr/o (kidney); read them carefully, letter by letter. Mistake: forgetting that one structure may have two roots, so both nephr/o and ren/o are correct for the kidney. Mistake: leaving the combining vowel in place before a vowel-starting suffix, which turns hepatitis into the wrong hepatoitis. Exit: (a) What does oste/o mean, and name one term that uses it? (b) Which root means stomach, and what is inflammation of the stomach called? Answers: oste/o means bone, as in osteoporosis or osteoarthritis; gastr/o means stomach, and inflammation of the stomach is gastritis.

lessons.title: Prefixes and suffixes
lessons.grammar_note: A prefix changes a term's meaning but a suffix usually sets its grammatical type - -itis makes a condition, -ectomy makes a procedure, and -ology makes a field of study.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define a set of high-frequency prefixes and suffixes and use them to both build and decode terms. Prefixes tend to signal location, number, time, or negation, while suffixes usually name a condition, a procedure, or a specialty, so together they frame whatever root sits in the middle. By the end you will be able to read a word such as pericarditis or anemia and account for every part. Warm-up: the prefixes hyper- and hypo- are opposites; which one means above normal and which means below normal? Keep that pair in mind, because the lesson pairs several opposites - fast against slow, around against through - and shows how a single swapped prefix can flip a term from one clinical meaning to its mirror image while the root stays the same.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Start with six common prefixes. Hyper- means excessive or above normal, and hypo- means deficient or below normal. Brady- means slow, and tachy- means fast. The pair a- and an- means without or absence of, where an- is used before a vowel. Peri- means around or surrounding. Now six common suffixes. The suffix -itis means inflammation. The suffix -ectomy means surgical removal, while -otomy (also written -tomy) means cutting into or making an incision. The suffix -ology, or -logy, means the study of. The suffix -emia means a blood condition. The suffix -pathy means disease, and -oma means a tumor or mass. Each prefix attaches to the front and each suffix to the end, so a term often reads as prefix plus root plus suffix. Because prefixes and suffixes are reused across every body system, mastering these twelve parts unlocks an enormous number of terms at once.

sections.heading: Key parts & examples
sections.text: See the parts combine. Hyper- plus glyc (sugar) plus -emia gives hyperglycemia, a blood sugar level above normal; swap in hypo- for hypoglycemia, below normal. Brady- plus cardi plus -a gives bradycardia, a slow heart rate, and tachy- gives tachycardia, a fast heart rate. The negating pair appears in apnea, a- plus -pnea (breathing), meaning without breathing, and in anemia, an- plus -emia, a blood condition marked by too few healthy red cells. Peri- plus cardi plus -itis gives pericarditis, inflammation around the heart. For procedures, append plus -ectomy gives appendectomy, removal of the appendix, while trache plus -otomy gives tracheotomy, a cut into the windpipe. For disease and growth, neur/o plus -pathy gives neuropathy, nerve disease, and carcin/o plus -oma gives carcinoma, a cancerous tumor. Each term is just a prefix, a root, and a suffix clicking together.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What do hyper- and hypo- mean? 2) Build a term for a fast heart rate from tachy-, cardi, and -a. 3) What is the difference between -ectomy and -otomy? 4) Decode pericarditis into its three parts. 5) What does -emia tell you, and give one example. 6) What does a- or an- add to a term? Answers: 1) hyper- means above normal and hypo- means below normal. 2) tachycardia. 3) -ectomy is surgical removal of a part, while -otomy is cutting into or making an incision. 4) peri- (around) + cardi (heart) + -itis (inflammation), inflammation around the heart. 5) -emia means a blood condition, as in anemia or hyperglycemia. 6) it means without or absence of, as in apnea, without breathing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: mixing up hyper- and hypo-, which are only a letter apart but describe opposite extremes - always read the full prefix. Mistake: confusing -ectomy (remove the part) with -otomy (only cut into it); the procedures are very different. Mistake: forgetting that an- is the form used before a vowel, so it is anemia, not aemia. Exit: (a) Which suffix names a surgical removal, and which names an incision? (b) What does the prefix peri- mean, and name one term that uses it? Answers: -ectomy names a surgical removal and -otomy names an incision; peri- means around, as in pericarditis or the pericardium around the heart.

questions.prompt: Building a term from the root 'gastr' and the suffix '-itis', the correct form is...
questions.explanation: The suffix -itis begins with a vowel, so the combining vowel is dropped, giving gastritis.

questions.prompt: The combining form 'oste/o' refers to...
questions.explanation: 'Oste/o' means bone, as in osteoporosis and osteoarthritis.

questions.prompt: The prefix 'peri-' means...
questions.explanation: 'Peri-' means around or surrounding, as in pericarditis.

questions.prompt: The suffix '-ology' (or '-logy') means...
questions.explanation: '-ology' means the study of, as in cardiology and neurology.

questions.prompt: A person with 'hyperglycemia' has a blood sugar level that is...
questions.explanation: 'Hyper-' means above normal, and -emia is a blood condition, so it is high blood sugar.

questions.prompt: The suffix '-oma' means...
questions.explanation: '-oma' means a tumor or mass, as in carcinoma or lipoma.

lessons.title: Terms organized by body system
lessons.grammar_note: Grouping roots by body system makes them stick - once you know cardi/o, angi/o, and vas/o all belong to the cardiovascular system, a new term in that family is easier to place.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sort common roots and terms into the body systems they describe, and recognize the specialty that studies each one. Organizing vocabulary by system turns a long flat list into a small map, so a new word arrives already connected to the others around it. By the end you will be able to place roots like pulmon/o, gastr/o, and neur/o in the right system and name a condition from each. Warm-up: a doctor who treats the heart and blood vessels works in which system? Keep that in mind, because this lesson tours five major systems - cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, musculoskeletal, and nervous - giving the key roots and one or two sample terms for each so you can see the same word-building rules at work across the whole body.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The cardiovascular system is the heart and blood vessels, with roots cardi/o (heart), angi/o and vas/o (vessel), arteri/o (artery), and ven/o (vein); its specialty is cardiology. The respiratory system moves air, with roots pulmon/o and pneum/o (lung), bronch/o (airway), trache/o (windpipe), and laryng/o (voice box); its specialty is pulmonology. The digestive system processes food, with roots gastr/o (stomach), enter/o (intestine), hepat/o (liver), and col/o (colon); its specialty is gastroenterology. The musculoskeletal system supports and moves the body, with roots oste/o (bone), arthr/o (joint), my/o (muscle), and chondr/o (cartilage); its specialties include orthopedics and rheumatology. The nervous system carries signals, with roots neur/o (nerve), encephal/o and cerebr/o (brain), and myel/o (spinal cord); its specialty is neurology. The same roots, prefixes, and suffixes you already know simply recombine within each system.

sections.heading: Key parts & examples
sections.text: Each system supplies familiar terms. Cardiovascular: cardiology (study of the heart), pericarditis (inflammation around the heart), and hypertension (high blood pressure). Respiratory: bronchitis (inflammation of the airways), pneumonia (infection of lung tissue), and dyspnea, dys- (difficult) plus -pnea (breathing), meaning labored breathing. Digestive: gastritis (inflammation of the stomach), hepatitis (inflammation of the liver), colitis (inflammation of the colon), and appendectomy (removal of the appendix). Musculoskeletal: arthritis (inflammation of a joint), osteoporosis (porous, weakened bone), and myalgia (muscle pain). Nervous: neuritis (inflammation of a nerve), neuropathy (nerve disease), and encephalitis (inflammation of the brain). Notice how -itis, -pathy, and -ology move from system to system unchanged, attaching to whichever root fits. That portability is the whole point: learn the parts once, then apply them wherever they are needed across the body.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which system do the roots cardi/o and angi/o belong to? 2) Name the specialty that studies the stomach and intestines. 3) Decode bronchitis into its parts. 4) Which root means lung, and name a lung infection. 5) Place encephal/o in a system and give one term that uses it. 6) What does myalgia mean? Answers: 1) the cardiovascular system. 2) gastroenterology. 3) bronch (airway) + -itis (inflammation), inflammation of the airways. 4) pulmon/o or pneum/o means lung, and pneumonia is a lung infection. 5) encephal/o (brain) is in the nervous system, as in encephalitis, inflammation of the brain. 6) muscle pain, from my/o (muscle) and -algia (pain).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming each body part has only one root, when many have two, such as pneum/o and pulmon/o for the lung or encephal/o and cerebr/o for the brain. Mistake: attaching a suffix to the wrong system's root and inventing a term that does not exist; check that the root and condition actually belong together. Mistake: forgetting that a shared suffix like -itis keeps the same meaning everywhere, so arthritis and hepatitis both mean inflammation. Exit: (a) Name the main roots of the respiratory system. (b) What condition is inflammation of the colon called? Answers: pulmon/o, pneum/o, bronch/o, trache/o, and laryng/o; inflammation of the colon is colitis.

lessons.title: Directional terms, body positions, and planes
lessons.grammar_note: Directional terms come in opposite pairs - anterior and posterior, superior and inferior, medial and lateral, proximal and distal - so learning one of each pair gives you the other for free.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use the standard directional terms, body positions, and anatomical planes that let clinicians describe exactly where something is. Everyday words like above, below, or near are too vague for medicine, so a precise shared vocabulary prevents dangerous confusion. By the end you will be able to say whether one structure is superior or inferior to another, name the plane that splits the body into left and right, and tell supine from prone. Warm-up: if the nose is toward the front of the head and the back of the skull is toward the rear, which single word describes the front position? Hold that thought, because directional terms are always given relative to the anatomical position - the body standing upright, facing forward, with palms turned to the front - which is the fixed reference every term below assumes.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Directional terms come in opposite pairs. Anterior (or ventral) means toward the front, and posterior (or dorsal) means toward the back. Superior means above or toward the head, and inferior means below or toward the feet. Medial means toward the midline of the body, and lateral means toward the side. Proximal means nearer the point of attachment or the trunk, and distal means farther from it. Superficial means near the surface, and deep means farther inside. Body positions describe how a patient lies: supine is face up, and prone is face down. Finally, three anatomical planes slice the body. The sagittal plane divides it into left and right parts, and a midsagittal plane gives equal halves. The frontal, or coronal, plane divides it into front and back parts. The transverse, or horizontal, plane divides it into upper and lower parts. These references stay fixed no matter how the patient is actually turned.

sections.heading: Key parts & examples
sections.text: Put the terms to work. The heart is superior to the stomach but inferior to the collarbone. The nose is anterior on the head, while the spine runs along the posterior of the trunk. The thumb is lateral to the little finger when the palm faces forward, and the breastbone is medial compared with the shoulder. The elbow is proximal to the wrist, because it is nearer the trunk, while the fingers are distal. The skin is superficial and the bones lie deep. For positions, a patient resting face up for an abdominal exam is supine, and one lying face down is prone. For planes, a sagittal cut through the body separates left from right; a frontal cut separates the face side from the back; and a transverse cut, like slicing a loaf, separates the upper body from the lower. Combining a plane with a direction, a surgeon might describe a lesion as lateral and superior on a transverse image.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which term means toward the midline, and which means toward the side? 2) Is the knee proximal or distal to the ankle? 3) Which plane divides the body into left and right parts? 4) What is the difference between supine and prone? 5) Give the opposite of superior. 6) The skin relative to the muscles beneath it is superficial or deep? Answers: 1) medial is toward the midline and lateral is toward the side. 2) proximal, because the knee is nearer the trunk than the ankle. 3) the sagittal plane. 4) supine is lying face up and prone is lying face down. 5) inferior. 6) superficial.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using everyday words like up or down instead of superior and inferior, which lose meaning once a patient is lying or turned. Mistake: swapping supine and prone; remember that supine faces up, like a cup holding soup. Mistake: confusing the frontal plane (front and back) with the sagittal plane (left and right). Mistake: forgetting that all terms assume the anatomical position, so left and right refer to the patient's own sides, not yours. Exit: (a) Name the three anatomical planes and what each divides. (b) Is the wrist proximal or distal to the elbow? Answers: sagittal (left and right), frontal or coronal (front and back), and transverse (upper and lower); the wrist is distal to the elbow.

lessons.title: Abbreviations, plurals, and pronunciation
lessons.grammar_note: Many medical plurals follow Latin and Greek patterns, not English - one vertebra becomes two vertebrae, one nucleus becomes two nuclei, and one diagnosis becomes two diagnoses.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read common clinical abbreviations, use medical plurals correctly, and pronounce unfamiliar terms with confidence. These finishing skills keep communication clear and safe, since a misread abbreviation or a wrong plural can change the meaning of a record. By the end you will recognize everyday shorthand, form the plural of Latin and Greek nouns, and sound out tricky letter combinations. Warm-up: if a medication is ordered twice a day, the chart may use the abbreviation bid - can you guess what tid might mean? Keep that in view, because this lesson also covers which abbreviations are considered unsafe and should be avoided, so you learn not only what shorthand means but also when writing a term out in full is the safer and more professional choice.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Abbreviations save time in charts and orders. Common ones include BP (blood pressure), HR (heart rate), Hx (history), Dx (diagnosis), Tx (treatment), and Rx (prescription). For timing and route, bid means twice a day, tid three times a day, prn as needed, po by mouth, npo nothing by mouth, and stat immediately. Plurals usually follow the word's original language. Words ending in -a often take -ae (vertebra to vertebrae). Words ending in -us often take -i (nucleus to nuclei, bronchus to bronchi). Words ending in -um often take -a (bacterium to bacteria, ovum to ova). Words ending in -is often take -es (diagnosis to diagnoses, metastasis to metastases). Words ending in -ix or -ex often take -ices (appendix to appendices). Pronunciation has its own patterns: ph sounds like f, ps and pn drop the p at the start of a word, ch often sounds like k, and c is soft before e, i, or y but hard before a, o, or u.

sections.heading: Key parts & examples
sections.text: See the rules in action. An order reading 'amoxicillin 500 mg po tid' means 500 milligrams by mouth three times a day, while 'npo after midnight' means nothing by mouth after midnight. Plurals: one vertebra and several vertebrae; one bronchus and two bronchi; a single bacterium and many bacteria; one diagnosis and two diagnoses; one appendix and several appendices. Pronunciation: pharynx begins with an f sound because of ph; psychology and pneumonia begin with a silent p; cholesterol starts with a k sound from ch; and in cephalic the c is soft (an s sound) before e, while in cardiac the c is hard (a k sound) before a. Safe practice also means avoiding error-prone shorthand: write 'units' rather than U, which can look like a zero; include a leading zero, writing 0.5 mg not .5 mg; and drop a trailing zero, writing 5 mg not 5.0 mg, so a missed decimal point cannot cause a tenfold overdose.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What do bid, tid, and prn mean? 2) Give the plural of diagnosis and of bronchus. 3) How is the ph in pharynx pronounced? 4) Why is a dose written 0.5 mg rather than .5 mg? 5) What does npo mean? 6) Is the c in cardiac hard or soft, and why? Answers: 1) twice a day, three times a day, and as needed. 2) diagnoses and bronchi. 3) like the letter f. 4) the leading zero makes the decimal point visible, preventing a reader from missing it and giving a tenfold overdose. 5) nothing by mouth. 6) hard (a k sound), because c is hard before a, o, or u.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding an English -s to a Latin noun, writing diagnosises instead of diagnoses or appendixes where appendices is expected. Mistake: trusting unsafe abbreviations; the letter U for units, a missing leading zero, or an extra trailing zero have all caused real dosing errors, so write them out when in doubt. Mistake: sounding out silent letters, saying the p in pneumonia or psychology. Mistake: assuming every abbreviation is universal, when some are ambiguous and vary by setting. Exit: (a) Give the singular and plural of vertebra and of nucleus. (b) Name one abbreviation habit that reduces medication errors. Answers: vertebra and vertebrae, nucleus and nuclei; using a leading zero and no trailing zero, or writing units in full instead of U, each reduce errors.

items.translation: the part of a term that carries its core meaning, usually a body part
items.example: In neurology, the root neur means nerve.

items.translation: a connecting letter, almost always o, that joins a root to a suffix or to another root
items.example: The o in gastroenterology links the roots gastr and enter.

items.translation: a word root written together with its combining vowel, shown as root/o
items.example: Cardi/o is the combining form for the heart.

items.translation: a part added to the front of a term to change its meaning, often location, number, time, or negation
items.example: In hypothermia, the prefix hypo- means below normal.

items.translation: a part added to the end of a term, often naming a condition, procedure, or specialty
items.example: In appendectomy, the suffix -ectomy means surgical removal.
Arthritis is inflammation of a joint.

items.translation: a suffix meaning surgical removal or excision
items.example: A nephrectomy is the removal of a kidney.

items.translation: the study of disease, from path/o (disease) and -logy (study of)
items.example: A pathology report describes the changes that disease has caused in a tissue sample.

questions.prompt: The combining form 'pulmon/o' belongs to which body system?
questions.explanation: 'Pulmon/o' means lung, part of the respiratory system.

questions.prompt: 'Gastroenterology' is the study of the...
questions.explanation: gastr (stomach) + enter (intestine) + -ology (study of).

questions.prompt: The directional term meaning 'toward the midline of the body' is...
questions.explanation: Medial means toward the midline; lateral means toward the side.

questions.prompt: The transverse plane divides the body into...
questions.explanation: The transverse (horizontal) plane separates upper from lower.

questions.prompt: To reduce medication errors, a dose of one half milligram is safest written as...
questions.explanation: Use a leading zero and no trailing zero, so 0.5 mg, to keep the decimal point visible.

questions.prompt: The plural of 'diagnosis' is...
questions.explanation: Words ending in -is take -es, giving diagnoses.
